commentary: Aquinas opens Book Five by observing that a principle and a cause are, in reality, the same underlying thing, though the two words differ in what they signify: 'principle' names an order of before and after, while 'cause' names an actual influence on the being of what it causes. Because order is most familiar to us in local motion, Aquinas traces how 'beginning' first meant the point in a magnitude or path from which motion starts, then, by extension, the point from which learning or any process proceeds most conveniently, which need not be the point that is first by nature. He works outward through further senses: the intrinsic first part from which a thing is generated (a ship's keel, a house's foundation, the heart or brain in an animal), the extrinsic source of a change (a parent, an insult that starts a quarrel), that whose will governs what is moved (magistrates, the ruling or 'architectonic' arts that command subordinate ones), and finally that from which a thing first becomes known, as the premises are the beginning of a demonstration. All these converge on one common note: a beginning is simply whatever is first, whether in being, in becoming, or in being known. Aquinas adds that some beginnings are intrinsic to the thing, such as nature, matter, and form, while others are extrinsic, such as intellect, will, and the end pursued, which moves both action and understanding.

Aquinas presents the four causes Aristotle distinguishes and stresses that the final cause required deliberate proof, since earlier natural philosophers had overlooked it entirely. Matter is that intrinsic, persisting stuff out of which something comes to be, such as bronze remaining bronze even after becoming a statue. Form is the pattern or definition that makes a thing what it is, whether as intrinsic shape or as an exemplar to be imitated. The efficient cause is the source from which change or rest first begins, and Aquinas here inserts Avicenna's fourfold division of agency into what perfects, what merely disposes matter, what assists a principal cause, and what supplies the very end and form of acting, as an architect does for a shipbuilder. The final cause is that for whose sake something occurs, and Aquinas shows this genuinely counts as a cause because 'why' questions are answered by naming it. He then draws out several consequences: several per se causes, not merely coincidental ones, can belong to one effect, since matter and agent cause differently; causes can be reciprocally causal, as exercise and good bodily condition are each cause of the other in different respects; and one and the same thing, through its presence or absence, can be cause of contrary outcomes, as a helmsman's presence brings safety and his absence brings wreck. Efficient and final causes correspond to each other, as do matter and form, each pair causing the other's being in a different way.

Having distinguished the four kinds of cause, Aquinas next shows that all the ways a cause is named reduce to those four, since letters cause syllables, matter causes artifacts, simple bodies cause mixtures, parts cause wholes, and premises cause conclusions, all in the manner of material causation, while other examples fall under the other three kinds. He then draws the further distinction between species of cause and modes of cause: species divide according to essentially different ways of causing, while modes concern the varying relations a cause of one and the same kind can bear to its effect. Aquinas lays out these modes in pairs: prior and posterior causes, as a remote universal cause like the sun stands behind a proximate particular cause like a father; per se causes as opposed to accidental ones, since Polyclitus causes the statue only because he happens to be its sculptor; and simple causes as opposed to composite ones, where several elements are named together. He notes, too, that accidental causation itself admits of degrees of remoteness, and that potential causes differ from actual causes in that particular actual causes exist and perish together with their effects, while causes taken according to potency need not. Multiplying these pairs yields, Aquinas explains, twelve distinct ways causes may be considered, even though the fundamental kinds of cause remain only four.

Aquinas draws four conditions from Aristotle's account of what makes something an element. First, an element must be a cause in the manner of intrinsic matter, so it belongs to material causation. Second, it must be that from which a thing is composed as its first and primary constituent, which distinguishes true elements from intermediate materials like bronze, itself made from something more basic. Third, an element must remain intrinsically present within the thing composed of it, unlike a contrary or privation from which something is merely said to come. Fourth, it must possess a single, indivisible species, so that however it is further divided, its parts remain of the same kind, as any portion of water is still water, unlike a syllable whose letters differ from one another. Aquinas illustrates this fourfold notion through letters as elements of speech, simple bodies as elements of mixtures, and, in demonstrations, the primary three-term syllogisms in which no middle term is drawn from a prior syllogism. He then explains a transferred, looser use of 'element' for whatever is one, small, and useful for many purposes, which led some thinkers to call the most universal things, such as genus, unity, or the point, elements. Aquinas notes this transferred usage is imprecise, since universals are not material components out of which particulars are built but rather predicate the substance of many things at once.

Aquinas explains that Aristotle traces 'nature' back to the birth or generation of living things, from which the word itself derives, and observes that strictly speaking only living things are said to be born, so this original sense applies properly to plants and animals and their parts. From this first meaning follow four more: the intrinsic principle from which growth first proceeds; the intrinsic source of motion present in a natural thing according to its own essence and not incidentally, as the physician's art is not the source of his own recovery insofar as he happens to be sick; the underlying matter, unshaped in itself, out of which natural things are made, which some early philosophers mistakenly took to be the only true nature; and the form or essence, since nothing is said to have attained its nature until it possesses its proper shape, form being the terminus toward which generation moves. Aquinas is careful to insist that nature, on every one of these senses, always names an intrinsic principle, never an external one. He concludes that nature in the primary and most proper sense is the form or essence of things that have within themselves, as such, a source of motion, while matter is called nature only because it is receptive of form, and generation only because it is a movement proceeding from and toward form.

Aquinas distinguishes four senses of the necessary. First, that without which a thing cannot live or continue to be, as breathing and food are necessary to an animal, functioning as a kind of contributing cause even though not the principal cause of life. Second, that without which some good cannot be attained or some evil avoided, as taking medicine is necessary for recovering health. Third, the compulsory or violent, whatever impedes a thing's own impulse or the will's own proposal, which is why necessity of this kind is called painful, since it opposes what we want, and also blameless, since we are only reproached for what we do willingly. Fourth, and most properly, that which cannot be otherwise than it is, necessary absolutely rather than merely in some respect. Aquinas shows that the other three senses all trace back to this fourth: compulsion is necessary because the one compelled cannot act otherwise; the first two senses are necessary because, given a certain end, life or good cannot come about except through them. He notes that demonstration depends on this strict necessity, since a demonstrated conclusion admits no alternative only if its premises are themselves necessary, and effects cannot follow necessarily from causes that are not. What is necessary in the fullest sense must be simple, incapable of being otherwise in any respect, which is why nothing violent or unnatural can belong to eternal, unmoving substances.

Aquinas first addresses unity that occurs by accident, as when 'musical' and 'Coriscus' are called one only because one happens to belong to the other, or when two accidents like 'musical' and 'just' are called one only because both happen to inhere in the same subject; such unity is never predicated universally, since accidents belong to individuals rather than to natures as such. He then turns to unity that belongs to things by their own nature, presenting five principal modes. Things are one by continuity, more truly so when the continuity is natural rather than produced by art, and a straight line is more fully one than a bent one, since only the straight line's motion is entirely simultaneous throughout. Things are one when their underlying subject does not differ in kind, whether considered as the nearest matter, like wine and water each being one, or as the ultimate matter into which many things are ultimately resolved, like all liquids being one as water. Things are one when they share a single genus divided by opposite differences, as man, horse, and dog are one as animals. Things are one when the definition expressing one thing's essence is inseparable from that of another. And things are most fully one, especially in the category of substance, when the very concept grasping their essence is utterly indivisible, admitting no composition at all, as with a point or with unity itself.

Aquinas shows how the five modes of essential unity discussed previously all reduce to a single root: whatever lacks division is called one precisely insofar as it lacks it, whether that indivision concerns quantity alone, an underlying subject, a genus, a definition, or, most fully, the very act of understanding a thing's essence. He adds a further nuance beyond mere indivision: something counts as a genuine, complete whole, and hence most truly one, not merely by being continuous but by possessing a single determinate form requiring an ordered arrangement of parts, as the pieces of a shoe are not truly one unless assembled into the shape and function of a shoe; for this reason the circle, being both continuous and complete in itself, is the most perfectly one of all figures. Aquinas then explains that unity is the very principle of number, since the first measure by which anything in a class is known counts as that class's basic unit, though this unit differs across different genera, being indivisible sometimes in quantity, sometimes in kind. Finally he presents the logical division of unity into oneness of number (shared matter), of species (shared definition), of genus (shared mode of predication), and of analogy or proportion (a shared relation between different pairs of things), noting that each later kind is broader than and implied by, but does not imply, the one before it.

Aquinas explains that being divides first into being per accidens and being per se, a division distinct from that between substance and accident, since even accidents themselves, considered absolutely, belong to being per se, while being per accidens concerns only the manner of predicating one thing of another, as when an accident is predicated of another accident, of its subject, or a subject of its accident, in every case because one thing merely happens to belong to another. Being per se, by contrast, corresponds exactly to the figures of predication, the categories, since being is said in as many ways as things are predicated, whether signifying substance, quality, quantity, or another mode; being cannot be a genus divided by differentiae, since nothing lies outside being to serve as such a differentia, so it is instead contracted to the different categories through the different ways of predicating that follow the different ways of being. Aquinas notes a further sense in which being and 'is' signify simply that a proposition is true, and not-being that it is false, a sense he calls posterior to and dependent on the first, since truth or falsity of speech follows from how things actually stand. Finally, being and its parts divide according to potency and actuality, since a thing may be said to be, or to have some attribute, either potentially or in complete actuality, as an image is potentially present in unshaped stone.

Aquinas presents four senses of substance drawn from common usage and philosophical opinion. First, the simple bodies and everything composed of them, animals, their organs, and even the beings some ancients revered as divine, all called substances because they are never predicated of a further subject while other things are predicated of them. Second, whatever, being intrinsic to such things, is the cause of their being, as the soul is the substance and cause of being of an animal. Third, the parts into which Platonists and Pythagoreans held such substances were ultimately resolved, such as surfaces, lines, points, and above all number, which they mistakenly regarded as the substance of everything, since removing it seemed to leave nothing; Aquinas rejects this, since what is universally required for a thing to exist need not itself be that thing's substance. Fourth, the quiddity or essence expressed by a thing's definition, which differs from form taken as a mere part, since essence includes the whole of what makes a thing what it is. Aquinas reduces these four to two fundamental senses: substance as the ultimate subject that is never itself predicated of anything else, a particular 'this something' existing separately and per se, and substance as the form or essence, that whereby a thing is what it is.

Aquinas here treats what is 'the same,' beginning with sameness by accident, as when 'pale' and 'musical' are called the same only because both happen to belong to one subject, or when a subject and its accident are called the same because one is predicated of the other, as 'Socrates' and 'musical Socrates' are loosely called the same though never universally, since accidents belong to individuals and not to natures universally. Sameness that holds by a thing's own nature, he explains, follows the very senses already given for essential unity, whether grounded in one matter or in one substance through continuity or through an indivisible, unified account. From this Aquinas draws an important conclusion: sameness is a kind of oneness, either of several things found to converge in some single respect, or of one thing considered as though it were more than one, as when something is said to be the same as itself, which requires the intellect to treat what is really one as two termini in order to conceive a relation at all; such self-identity is therefore a relation of reason rather than a real relation, since a real relation would generate an infinite regress of further relations relating the thing to its own sameness. Things are called 'other' when their kinds, matters, or essential definitions are multiple, the direct opposite of sameness in every mode.

Aquinas explains that 'different' properly applies only to things that, while agreeing in some respect, whether numerically, specifically, generically, or by proportion, nevertheless diverge in another; strictly, only things sharing some common ground are called different, since things sharing nothing at all differ, as it were, entirely through themselves rather than through anything else. Most properly different are things sharing the same genus yet divided by contrary differentiae, or things whose species are themselves contraries. Turning to 'like,' Aquinas presents three grades: things undergoing literally the same modification, things merely undergoing some modification each, whether the same or different, and, most properly, things sharing a single quality outright, such as two white objects. Something counts as more fully like another the more of the contrarieties relevant to alteration it shares, and especially when the shared quality is that thing's own proper quality rather than one merely held in common more loosely, as air resembles fire chiefly through heat, its own proper quality, rather than through some lesser point of overlap. Aquinas closes by noting that 'unlike' is simply the opposite of 'like' throughout, following the same distinctions in reverse, since wherever quality fails to converge in the relevant respects, dissimilarity rather than likeness results.

Aquinas distinguishes four kinds of opposition: contradiction, contrariety, privation and possession, and relative terms, explaining that things are opposed either through dependency, which grounds relative opposition, or through some manner of removal, which yields three further grades depending on how much removal leaves behind. Sheer negation removes everything, leaving nothing; privation removes an attribute while leaving the subject that could have possessed it; and contrariety removes while leaving both subject and genus intact, since true contraries must share a common genus and often a common recipient subject. Aquinas shows that opposition can also be recognized through comparison to motion, since the terms from which and to which a change proceeds are opposed, as generation of the pale proceeds from the not-pale, and through comparison to a subject, since attributes that cannot both belong to one and the same receptive thing at once must be opposed, either themselves or the things underlying them. Contraries proper are things within one genus that differ maximally, whether absolutely, within a genus, or within a species, and secondary contraries are named by their relation to these, whether by possessing, receiving, producing, or losing genuine contraries. Finally, Aquinas lays out five ways things are called different in species: belonging to one genus without subordination, dividing one genus by a differentia, having subjects marked by contrary differentiae, being distinct ultimate species of one genus, or being contrary accidents unable to coexist in one subject.

Aquinas shows that 'prior' and 'posterior' always presuppose some determinate beginning or principle, nearness to which makes a thing prior, whether that principle is fixed absolutely by nature or only relative to some further consideration, place, or particular people. He works through several orders in which this nearness is measured: place, where nearness to a naturally determined center or extreme, such as the world's middle or the heavens, makes a thing prior; time, where past events are prior the farther they lie from the present, but future events are prior the nearer they lie to it; motion, where nearness to the first mover makes a thing prior, so a child is prior to a grown man as nearer to the generative source, and this order extends to voluntary affairs, where the more powerful, whose will others must follow, counts as prior; and arrangement, as in a chorus or the strings of a lyre, where nearness to some fixed reference point determines priority. Aquinas then distinguishes priority in cognition, where universals are prior according to reason though individuals are prior to sense perception, and priority in nature and substance, which Plato used, whereby whatever can exist without other things while those others cannot exist without it is prior; this final sense, Aquinas notes, is ultimately what all the other modes of priority are reduced to, since what is prior never depends on what is posterior, whether the independence concerns generation or dissolution.

Aquinas distinguishes active from passive potency as the two fundamental senses of power: active potency is a source of motion or change located in one thing insofar as it produces change in another, or in the same thing considered as other than itself, as the art of building resides in the builder rather than in the building; passive potency is, correspondingly, a source enabling a thing to be moved or affected by another. He notes a further refinement, that potency sometimes names merely the capacity to undergo or produce some effect at all, and sometimes more strictly the capacity to do so well or as intended, so that one who walks or speaks poorly may be said, in this stricter sense, not truly to be able to walk or speak. Aquinas also distinguishes states of firm resistance to corruption or alteration as a kind of potency, since durability against destructive forces reflects a positive strength rather than a mere absence of weakness. He then treats 'possible' and 'impossible' as used without reference to any real potency at all, but according to logical necessity: the impossible is whatever has a contrary that is necessarily true, as with an incommensurable diagonal, while the possible is whatever has no contrary that is necessarily false. Aquinas concludes that every derivative sense of potency and possibility ultimately refers back to this primary active potency, a genuine source of change in another thing, or in the same thing considered as other.

Aquinas explains that quantity is whatever admits division into constituent parts, each of which is naturally capable of being one and a determinate 'this,' distinguishing this properly quantitative division from the resolution of a mixed body into elements present only virtually rather than actually within it. Quantity divides first into plurality, divisible into discontinuous parts and hence numerable, and magnitude, divisible into continuous parts and hence measurable, itself further specified as length, breadth, or depth according to whether continuity holds in one, two, or three dimensions, with number, line, surface, and solid arising as the limited or determinate versions of these. Aquinas then distinguishes quantity that belongs to a thing per se as its very substance, as a line is essentially a quantity, from quantity understood as an attribute or affection of such substantial quantities, as much and little, long and short, broad and narrow are affections respectively of number, line, and surface. He notes that great and small, and their comparative forms, belong to quantity by nature but are also transferred to other things. Finally he distinguishes two ways something is quantitative merely by accident: because it is an attribute of a quantified subject, as the musical is a quantum only because it belongs to a subject that is quantified, or because it is divisible only insofar as something else to which it is intrinsically tied, such as the magnitude traversed, is divisible, as motion and time are called quantities only in this derivative, posterior way.

Aquinas distinguishes four senses of quality. The primary and proper sense is the differentia of a thing's essence, that by which one answers what sort a thing is within its genus, as man is qualified as two-footed and the circle as having no angles, so that the very differentia constituting a substance's kind is itself called a quality. A second sense applies to the unchanging objects of mathematics, as numbers are called qualified insofar as they are composite or incomposite, or resemble plane or solid figures through repeated multiplication, a quality that belongs to their essence beyond bare quantity. Third, quality names the changeable affections of movable substances, such as heat, cold, whiteness, and blackness, in respect of which bodies are said to alter, corresponding to the sensible qualities through which alteration properly occurs. Fourth, quality names virtue and vice, and more broadly good and evil, especially as found in living, purposive beings, since virtue and vice mark differences in how a thing acts or is acted upon well or badly. Aquinas reduces these four to two principal senses, the differentia of essence being primary, with mathematical quality falling under it as a kind of essential differentia, while the affections of things in motion form the second principal sense, under which virtue and vice fall as differentiae specifying activity as good or defective, a distinction found most fully in beings capable of deliberate choice.

Aquinas distinguishes three basic modes of relation. The first concerns number, as double relates to half and multiple to submultiple, whether the numerical relation to unity or to another number is definite, like the sesquialter ratio of three to two, or indefinite, like the merely exceeding relation of a greater quantity to a lesser. The second concerns active and passive potency, as the heating relates to the heatable, and more generally every agent to what it acts upon. The third concerns measure and the measurable, as the knowable relates to knowledge and the perceptible to perception, a relation that, unlike the first two, does not hold reciprocally, since only the measurable is related to its measure and not conversely, because truth is measured by the reality known rather than the reverse. Aquinas explains the rationale behind this threefold division: one thing can be ordered to another according to being, which yields the third mode, according to active and passive power, which yields the second, or according to quantity capable of measurement, which yields the first. He also notes that equal, like, and same are relative according to unity taken absolutely rather than through comparison of numbers. Finally, some things are called relative only secondarily, either because their genus is relative, as medicine is relative because science is, because an abstract term is relative since its corresponding concrete term is, as equality is relative because the equal is, or merely by accident, as a man happens to be double something.

Aquinas presents three senses of the complete. First, that outside which no part belonging to it can be found, as a complete span of time is one lacking no portion proper to it. Second, that which, in respect of excellence within its own kind, cannot be surpassed and lacks nothing belonging to its proper virtue, as a complete physician or flute player lacks nothing pertaining to skill in that craft; Aquinas notes this sense is even transferred, by an ironic extension, to bad things, so that a thoroughgoing thief or slanderer is called 'perfect' at being what he is, since virtue in general is what makes a thing good and its activity good, and the transferred usage mimics this structure even where the activity itself is vicious. Third, whatever has attained its end is called complete, since an end is something ultimate, and this too is stretched, by resemblance rather than truth, to things utterly ruined or destroyed, and even to death, called an end only because it is a terminus, not because it is genuinely that for the sake of which anything occurs. Aquinas observes that only the first principle, God, is complete absolutely and without qualification, lacking nothing in any respect and needing nothing further, while other things are called complete only relative to their own genus, as a man is called complete upon attaining happiness.

Aquinas identifies four senses of limit. First, the outermost point of a thing, beyond which none of its own parts can be found and within which every part of it lies, as a point limits a line and a surface limits a body. Second, one extreme of a motion or action, specifically the terminus toward which the change tends rather than that from which it proceeds, though sometimes both extremes are loosely called limits, since every motion lies between two termini. Third, that for the sake of which something occurs, the ultimate object of an intention, corresponding to the terminus of motion in the practical order. Fourth, the substance or essence of a thing, expressed by its definition, since a definition is the terminus of cognition, the point beyond which nothing further need be sought to know what a thing is, and, because knowledge proceeds by the knower's assimilation to the thing known, what limits knowledge of a thing in this way must also, in some sense, limit the thing itself. Aquinas concludes by comparing limit to beginning: limit has as many senses as beginning and more, since every beginning is itself a kind of limit, but not every limit counts as a beginning, for the terminus toward which a motion tends is a limit yet in no way its starting principle.

Aquinas treats together 'that in virtue of which' and 'in virtue of itself.' The former has several senses corresponding to the senses of cause: the form or substance of a thing, as the good itself is that in virtue of which a man is good; the proximate subject in which an attribute naturally resides, as color exists in virtue of a surface; and, more loosely, the end for which, or the reason why, something occurs. 'In virtue of itself' likewise divides into several senses. First, the very essence of a thing, since Callias is, in virtue of himself, Callias and whatever it was for him to be Callias. Second, whatever is included in a thing's definition, as Callias is in virtue of himself an animal, since animal belongs to what he essentially is. Third, whatever a subject receives directly, in itself or in one of its parts, as a surface is white in virtue of itself, or a man is alive in virtue of himself because the soul, in which life directly resides, is a part of him. Fourth, whatever has no cause beyond itself, as man, despite having several partial causes such as animality and two-footedness, is nonetheless man in virtue of himself without further explanation. Fifth, whatever belongs to a thing considered strictly alone and apart from everything else, as when something is said to exist 'in virtue of itself' meaning simply by itself, in isolation.

Aquinas explains that disposition names the arrangement of the parts of something that has parts, whether that arrangement concerns place, potency, or kind, and observes that some determinate positioning or ordering is implied even by the word itself. He distinguishes three modes corresponding to the different ways parts can be ordered: an ordering according to place, which falls under the category of position or situs; an ordering according to power or capacity, whereby a thing is disposed well or badly, as through health or sickness, which falls under the first species of quality; and an ordering according to the specific form or shape of the whole, which falls under quantity, since some quantities, like lines, surfaces, bodies, and place, admit position among their parts, while others, like number and time, do not. Because this brief chapter treats a term of relatively narrow philosophical weight compared to the great terms surrounding it, such as unity, being, and substance, Aquinas moves through it economically, emphasizing chiefly that disposition always signifies some kind of order among parts, whatever the respect in which that order is considered, rather than developing an extended set of further distinctions, since the underlying notion, unlike quantity or quality themselves, does not constitute one of the primary categories but only a modification found within them.

Aquinas explains that 'having' or 'holding' bears several senses. First, to treat a thing according to one's own nature or impulse, as fever is said to have a man, tyrants to have their cities, and a person to have the clothes he wears, since in each case the haver directs or governs what is had. Second, that in which something exists as in a receptive subject is said to have it, as bronze has the shape of a statue and a body has a disease, this sense embracing the having of any accident, quality, or form whatsoever. Third, whatever contains is said to have what it contains, as a vessel has the liquid within it, a city its inhabitants, and a ship its sailors, and in this sense a whole is said to have its parts, since it contains them much as a place contains what occupies it, though a whole, unlike a place, is not divided from its parts as a place is divided from what it holds. Fourth, whatever prevents a thing from moving or acting according to its own natural impulse is said to have it, as pillars are said to have the weights pressing upon them, and, in poetic language, Atlas is said to have the heavens, a myth Aquinas traces back to an astronomer who studied the heavenly motions closely. Aquinas notes finally that 'being in something' parallels 'having' point for point.

Aquinas distinguishes several senses in which one thing is said to come from another. First, and most properly, from matter, whether the most general kind, as everything meltable is said to come from water broadly considered, or the specific and proximate matter, as a statue comes from bronze in particular. Second, from the first moving principle, as a fight comes from an insult that provoked it. Third, from the composite of matter and form, taken as a whole, as parts come from a whole and verses come from an entire poem, this sense working in the direction of resolution rather than composition, since form is the end toward which generation moves, and what is complete is precisely what has attained its form. Fourth, as a species comes from a part of the specific formula, as man comes from 'two-footed' and a syllable from a letter, which Aquinas distinguishes from the material sense because here the composition concerns a part of the intelligible form itself rather than sensible matter. He notes a fifth, looser use whereby something is said to come from another because it comes from some part of that other, as a child comes from father and mother, and finally a sixth sense involving mere succession in time without any real transformation, as night is said to come from day, or a voyage from the equinox, simply because one follows the other.

Aquinas distinguishes several senses of 'part.' In the broadest sense, whatever a quantity can in any way be divided into counts as a part, so that two is, loosely speaking, a part of three; more strictly, only that which measures the whole exactly is called its part, so that two is not, in this stricter sense, a part of three, though it is a part of four, since twice two makes four. Beyond quantity, the elements into which a kind divides, apart from any consideration of quantity, are also called parts, so that the species are said to be parts of their genus. Further, the constituents into which a whole, understood either as a form or as the concrete thing possessing that form, is divided or of which it is composed count as parts, as both the bronze, serving as matter, and the characteristic angle, belonging to the form, are parts of a bronze cube. Finally, the constituents included within the definition explaining what a thing is are also called its parts, which is why genus can be called a part of species in this sense, even though, taken in the second sense above, species is rather said to be a part of genus. Aquinas notes that the third sense concerns parts of the concrete thing itself, whether of the species or of the individual, while the fourth concerns parts belonging strictly to the intelligible formula.

Aquinas explains that a whole is, first, that from which none of the parts naturally belonging to it is missing, and, second, that which so contains what it contains that these form a genuine unity, which happens in two ways. In one way, as a universal whole, where each of the things contained is itself, individually, the very thing predicated as whole, as man, horse, and any other animal are each simply an animal, so that the universal is predicated of each part taken separately. In the other way, as a continuous and limited whole, a genuine unity composed of several parts, more fully a whole when those parts exist in it potentially, as in a continuous magnitude, than when they exist there only actually side by side, as stones piled in a heap, and more fully a whole when the unity is natural rather than produced merely by art. Aquinas notes a further distinction bearing on how position affects such wholes: things like water or wine, whose parts can be rearranged without altering the thing at all, are properly called 'totals' and spoken of with 'all' rather than 'whole'; things like a man or a house, whose determinate arrangement of parts is essential to what they are, are properly called wholes; and things like wax or a garment, which retain their underlying material through rearrangement even while losing their particular shape, admit both descriptions at once.

Aquinas lays out the conditions something must meet to be properly called mutilated or maimed. It must first be a quantitative whole capable of division into parts, since a universal whole cannot be mutilated merely by the loss of one of its species. It must further be divisible into unlike, distinguishable parts, so that homogeneous wholes like water or fire, whose parts do not differ from one another, cannot properly be mutilated, and it must possess a determinate position among those parts, which is why a musical harmony, though built of unlike high and low notes, still cannot be called mutilated, since removing one note does not leave a maimed harmony behind but simply a different arrangement. Two-part things cannot be mutilated by losing one part, since what is removed is never merely equal to what remains; and no number can be mutilated at all, since removing or adding even a single unit changes what kind of number results, whereas mutilation requires that the thing's substance survive the loss, as a cup remains recognizably a cup even after part of it is broken away. Finally, Aquinas specifies that the part lost must be an extremity rather than a central portion, and one that does not naturally grow back, which is why losing a hand or foot counts as mutilation while losing hair, which regenerates, or a spleen, which lies centrally, does not.

Aquinas distinguishes four senses of genus or race. First, the continuous generation of things sharing one and the same species, as one speaks of the human race continuing so long as generation among men persists. Second, that from which things first proceed as from their begetter, as the Hellenes are named for their descent from Hellen, a sense drawn more often from the father than the mother, though sometimes, as with the Pleiades, from a female ancestor. Third, genus functions as the common subject underlying specifically different accidents, as surface is genus to plane figures and solid to solid figures, this sense resembling matter, since the proper subject is placed in the definition of an accident much as genus is placed in the definition of a species. Fourth, and most properly for definitions, genus names the first element placed in a definition, predicated in answer to 'what is it,' of which the differentiae function as further qualifications, as animal stands to man. Aquinas reduces the third and fourth senses to a single underlying idea, genus functioning after the manner of matter to the differentia's manner of form. He then distinguishes two ways things are 'other in genus': through having irreducibly different proximate subjects, which concerns the natural philosopher, or through falling under different categories of predication altogether, which concerns the logician, since the categories neither reduce into one another nor into some further common genus.

Aquinas distinguishes the false first as it concerns things themselves, in two ways: either because a proposition about a matter simply cannot, or in some case does not, hold true, as an impossible falsehood like a commensurable diagonal is always false while a merely contingent falsehood, like someone sitting who in fact is standing, is false only sometimes; or because something real is naturally apt to appear other than it is or to appear as something that does not exist at all, as a shadow-picture or a dream produces a likeness without being the reality it resembles. Turning to false accounts, Aquinas explains that a definition is false, strictly, only when applied to something other than what it truly defines, since the very same definition true of one thing is false of another, as the definition of a circle is false when applied to a triangle; he uses this to refute Antisthenes, who denied that falsehood or even contradiction was possible on the mistaken assumption that only a thing's own proper definition could ever be predicated of it, whereas something can, in a qualified way, truly bear an account belonging properly to something else. Finally, a man is called false who is disposed toward, and delights in, producing false accounts for their own sake, which is why the argument in the Hippias confusing mere capacity to deceive with being habitually false is mistaken, since even the prudent man can deceive without thereby being a false man.

Aquinas distinguishes two senses of accident. The first names whatever truly belongs to a subject yet neither necessarily nor even usually, but only in the fewest cases, having no determinate or per se cause but only some incidental, chance cause, as a man digging a hole to plant something happens upon buried treasure, or a musician happens also to be pale; neither outcome follows from what the man was actually doing, and Aquinas notes there is no necessary connection or even any consistent frequency binding the two. Similarly, a voyage that lands unintentionally at Aegina, driven there by a storm rather than by design, illustrates accidental causation, since the sailor's arrival follows not from his purpose in sailing but from an entirely extraneous cause. The second sense names whatever belongs to a subject per se, in virtue of what that subject is, yet still does not belong to its essence or substance, as a triangle's having angles equal to two right angles belongs to it necessarily and always, yet does not enter into the definition of what a triangle is. Aquinas notes the crucial difference between the two senses: accidents of the first kind can never be perpetual, since by nature they occur only rarely, while accidents of the second kind can indeed be eternal, following with strict necessity from the thing's nature even though they remain, properly speaking, outside its essence.
